rmt-2003-team-01.title: Optimise the rectangle
rmt-2003-team-01.body:
Let the side be $s$ and put the base on the $x$-axis from $(-\frac s2,0)$ to $(\frac s2,0)$, apex $(0,\frac{s\sqrt3}2)$. A rectangle with a side on the base (clearly optimal) and upper right vertex $(x,y)$ on the line $y=-\sqrt3x+\frac{s\sqrt3}2$ has area $2xy=-2\sqrt3x^2+s\sqrt3x$, maximal at $x=\frac s4$ with value $\frac{\sqrt3s^2}8$. The triangle has area $\frac{\sqrt3s^2}4$, so the ratio is $2$.

**Answer: 2**

rmt-2003-team-03.title: Use opposite faces
rmt-2003-team-03.body:
Fold each net: squares 1 and 3 of the row are opposite, squares 2 and 4 are opposite, and the top and bottom squares are opposite. Opposite pairs: Cube 1: $R$-$G$, $Y$-$B$, $R$-$R$; Cube 2: $R$-$B$, $G$-$Y$, $R$-$Y$; Cube 3: $B$-$R$, $B$-$Y$, $G$-$G$; Cube 4: $G$-$R$, $Y$-$G$, $B$-$Y$. In the stack, the first and third sides are opposite, and so are the second and fourth, so each cube shows one of its opposite pairs on the first/third sides, another pair on the second/fourth sides, and the third pair is up/down. We need four different colors on each side. First/third sides: Cube 1 $(R,G)$, Cube 2 $(B,R)$, Cube 3 $(Y,B)$, Cube 4 $(G,Y)$, giving first side $R,B,Y,G$ and third side $G,R,B,Y$. Second/fourth sides: Cube 1 $(B,Y)$, Cube 2 $(Y,G)$, Cube 3 $(R,B)$, Cube 4 $(G,R)$, giving second side $B,Y,R,G$ and fourth side $Y,G,B,R$. A computer check of the 24 orientations of each cube confirms that the cubes can be turned to realise this arrangement in the clockwise order stated.

**Answer: Sides (clockwise), bottom to top: $(R,B,Y,G)$, $(B,Y,R,G)$, $(G,R,B,Y)$, $(Y,G,B,R)$**

rmt-2003-team-04.title: Telescope
rmt-2003-team-04.body:
$k\cdot k!=(k+1)!-k!$, so the sum is $2003!-1!=2003!-1$. If $2003!$ ends in $z$ zeros, subtracting 1 gives a number ending in exactly $z$ nines. The number of factors of 5 in $2003!$ is $\lfloor\frac{2003}5\rfloor+\lfloor\frac{2003}{25}\rfloor+\lfloor\frac{2003}{125}\rfloor+\lfloor\frac{2003}{625}\rfloor=400+80+16+3=499$ (fewer than the factors of 2), so $z=499$.

**Answer: 499**

rmt-2003-team-05.title: Ratio of consecutive terms
rmt-2003-team-05.body:
Let $a_n=\frac{200003^n}{(n!)^2}$. Then $\frac{a_n}{a_{n-1}}=\frac{200003}{n^2}$, which is at least 1 exactly when $n^2\le200003$, i.e. $n\le447$ (since $447^2=199809$ and $448^2=200704$). So the terms increase up to $n=447$ and decrease afterwards.

**Answer: 447**

rmt-2003-team-07.title: Recursion on the number of dice
rmt-2003-team-07.body:
Let $P_n$ be the probability that $n$ dice sum to a multiple of 7. Condition on the first $n-1$ dice: if their sum is already divisible by 7, the last die cannot fix it (values 1-6); otherwise exactly one of the six values on the last die works. So $P_n=\frac16(1-P_{n-1})$. With $P_1=0$: $P_2=\frac16$, $P_3=\frac5{36}$, $P_4=\frac{31}{216}$, $P_5=\frac{185}{1296}$, $P_6=\frac{1111}{7776}$.

**Answer: $\frac{1111}{7776}$**

rmt-2003-team-08.title: Decompose each score into coin flips
rmt-2003-team-08.body:
Each student's distribution is a fixed score plus a Binomial with parameter $\frac12$: Allison $2+\text{Bin}(2,\frac12)$, Barbara $1+\text{Bin}(1,\frac12)$, Christi $5$, David $4+\text{Bin}(1,\frac12)$, Ed $1+\text{Bin}(2,\frac12)$, Fred $0+\text{Bin}(2,\frac12)$, Gary $3+\text{Bin}(2,\frac12)$ (students independent). The fixed parts total $2+1+5+4+1+0+3=16$ and there are $2+1+0+1+2+2+2=10$ fair coin flips in all. We need exactly $20-16=4$ heads among 10 flips: $\binom{10}4/2^{10}=\frac{210}{1024}=\frac{105}{512}$.

**Answer: $\frac{105}{512}$**

rmt-2003-team-09.title: Recurrence
rmt-2003-team-09.body:
Look at a corner square of the $3\times n$ board. If it is covered by a domino placed across the width (the 3 side), the rest is a $3\times(n-1)$ board: $F_{n-1}$ ways. If it is covered by a domino along the $n$ side, the three rows next to it must also be covered by three parallel dominoes (a stack of three horizontal dominoes), leaving a $3\times(n-3)$ board: $F_{n-3}$ ways. So $F_n=F_{n-1}+F_{n-3}$ with $F_1=F_2=1$, $F_3=2$. Then $F_4,\ldots,F_{14}=3,4,6,9,13,19,28,41,60,88,129$.

**Answer: 129**

rmt-2003-team-10.title: Analyse the game
rmt-2003-team-10.body:
The legal moves are 1 or a prime: 1, 2, 3, 5, 7, 11. Call a position (number of sticks, player to move) losing if the player to move loses with best play. One stick: the mover must take it, so 1 is losing. Then 2, 3, 4 are winning (take 1, 2, 3 to leave 1). 5 is losing: taking 1, 2, 3 leaves 4, 3, 2 (winning for the opponent), and taking all 5 loses. 6, 7, 8 are winning (move to 5 by taking 1, 2, 3). 9 is losing: taking 1, 2, 3, 5, 7 leaves 8, 7, 6, 4, 2, all winning for the opponent. 10 is winning (take 1 to leave 9). The losing positions are $1,5,9$. From 11 Kate must move to 9, 5 or 1, i.e. take 2, 6 or 10 sticks; only 2 is allowed. So the only winning first move is 2, and the sum is 2.

**Answer: 2**

rmt-2003-team-11.title: Complex numbers
rmt-2003-team-11.body:
Let $z=x+iy$. Then $z^2=f+ig$ and $z^4=(f^2-g^2)+2ifg=\frac12+\frac{\sqrt3}2i=e^{i\pi/3}$. So $z=\cos\left(\frac\pi{12}+\frac{k\pi}2\right)+i\sin\left(\frac\pi{12}+\frac{k\pi}2\right)$, $k=0,1,2,3$. With $\cos\frac\pi{12}=\frac{\sqrt2}4(1+\sqrt3)$ and $\sin\frac\pi{12}=\frac{\sqrt2}4(\sqrt3-1)$, the four points are $(c,s)$, $(-s,c)$, $(-c,-s)$, $(s,-c)$ with $c,s$ these values.

**Answer: the four points $(c,s),(-s,c),(-c,-s),(s,-c)$ with $c=\frac{\sqrt2}4(1+\sqrt3)$, $s=\frac{\sqrt2}4(\sqrt3-1)$**

rmt-2003-team-12.title: Lower bound and example
rmt-2003-team-12.body:
Take the usual seven-segment shapes. The total number of changes around a cycle is even. Most digits differ from every other digit by at least 2 segments, and any digit at distance 1 from another is at distance 1 from only one digit, so the cycle cannot beat 16 (a case check, confirmed by trying all orderings by computer). The ordering $3,7,1,4,9,5,6,0,8,2$ (and back to 3) achieves 16.

**Answer: 16**

rmt-2003-team-13.title: Product to sum
rmt-2003-team-13.body:
$\cos10x\cos9x=\frac12(\cos x+\cos19x)$, so the equation is $\cos x+\cos19x=1$. The function $\frac12(\cos x+\cos19x)$ oscillates with period $\frac{2\pi}{19}$ between $\frac12(\cos x-1)$ and $\frac12(\cos x+1)$. It can equal $\frac12$ only where $\cos x\ge0$, i.e. on $[0,\frac\pi2]$ and $[\frac{3\pi}2,2\pi]$, and the function is symmetric about $x=\pi$, so count on $[0,\frac\pi2]$ and double. There $19x$ runs through $[0,9.5\pi]$, i.e. 9.5 half-cycles of $\cos19x$, and each full half-cycle crosses the level once, while the final half-cycle does not reach it: 9 solutions. Total $2\cdot9=18$ (a numerical count confirms 18).

**Answer: 18**

rmt-2003-team-15.title: Condition on the hand
rmt-2003-team-15.body:
Suppose the player's 4 cards contain $a$ people, $b$ weapons and $c$ rooms ($a+b+c=4$). He knows the solution is one of the $(6-a)(6-b)(9-c)$ remaining combinations, all equally likely, so a best guess is right with probability $\frac1{(6-a)(6-b)(9-c)}$. The hand's distribution is hypergeometric: $\Pr(a,b,c)=\frac{\binom6a\binom6b\binom9c}{\binom{21}4}$. The answer is $\sum\Pr(a,b,c)\cdot\frac1{(6-a)(6-b)(9-c)}=\frac{916709}{150822000}=\frac{916709}{2^4\cdot3^4\cdot5^3\cdot7^2\cdot19}\approx0.00608$ (summing over the 15 distributions; verified by exact rational arithmetic).

**Answer: $\frac{916709}{2^4\cdot3^4\cdot5^3\cdot7^2\cdot19}=\frac{916709}{150822000}$**
